question: When a blood vessel gets injured, what is the main job of primary haemostasis?

question: A nurse is getting a patient ready for a pacemaker insertion. What is the very first thing that must be done?

options.B: Program the pacemaker to a high heart rate

question: Why is keeping a close eye on blood pressure so important right after brain surgery?

question: What does 'informed consent' actually mean for a client undergoing a health screening?

options.A: They agree to take any medication prescribed after the test

question: What usually happens to uterine fibroids after a woman goes through menopause?

options.B: They rapidly grow larger and turn malignant
options.C: They multiply and spread to other organs
options.D: They usually shrink due to lower hormone levels

question: During continuous bladder irrigation, which finding means you need to take action right away?

question: A maternity ward protocol for treating postpartum hemorrhage is best described as what?

question: Why should soft pillows and stuffed animals be kept out of an infant's crib?

options.A: They create a suffocation and entrapment hazard

question: What two main changes happen in the blood during asphyxia?

options.D: Low glucose and high lactic acid

question: Why are newborn babies and burn patients at higher risk of chemical absorption from skin antiseptics?

question: What CD4 count marks the official shift from HIV to AIDS?

options.A: Below 1,000 cells/mm³
options.B: Below 500 cells/mm³
options.C: Below 200 cells/mm³
options.D: Below 800 cells/mm³

question: What classic structural change happens to the brain tissue in CJD?

options.A: Massive swelling of the blood vessels
options.B: Excessive growth of new nerve endings
options.C: Development of sponge-like holes
options.D: Hardening of the protective skull bone

question: Why are drug doses typically much smaller when given intrathecally compared to orally?

options.A: The liver breaks down the medicine much faster in the spinal cord
options.B: The stomach acid destroys most of the oral medication before absorption
options.C: The drug goes directly to the central nervous system without being filtered first
options.D: The blood-brain barrier absorbs most of the drug before it works

question: Why is teaching self-examination important in male reproductive care?

options.A: It is the only reliable way to diagnose a urinary tract infection
options.B: It replaces the need for any future professional medical visits
options.C: It helps patients detect early changes like lumps or swelling
options.D: It prevents the normal age-related decrease in testosterone

explanation: Correct! Self-exams empower patients to notice small changes right away, leading to quicker medical help and better health results.

question: Which main chemical messenger in the brain do most sedative drugs target to slow things down?

options.A: Acetylcholine
options.B: Gamma-aminobutyric acid
options.C: Norepinephrine
options.D: Dopamine

explanation: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the body's natural brake pedal. Sedatives step on this pedal to help calm brain activity. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the role of a neurotransmitter at a synapse?

options.A: To physically connect the dendrite of one cell to the axon of another
options.B: To chemically bridge the gap and transmit the signal to the next cell
options.C: To generate the original resting membrane potential
options.D: To insulate the axon with a protective fatty layer

question: What is the primary purpose of doing a routine Pap smear?

options.A: To screen for precancerous cellular changes on the cervix
options.B: To diagnose a severe bacterial urinary tract infection
options.C: To measure circulating levels of reproductive hormones
options.D: To test for active yeast infections in the vagina

question: During which phase of cancer development do cells gain aggressive traits and learn to spread?

options.A: Progression

question: What is the core belief behind occupational health?

options.A: Workers should accept all workplace risks as part of the job.

question: Lab results show a patient has large (macrocytic) red blood cells. Which vitamin shortage should you check for first?

options.A: Vitamin B12 or folate
options.B: Vitamin D and calcium

question: When a large amount of fluid is being drained, what vital sign change must a nurse watch out for?

question: Why does a nurse need to ask when a patient's symptoms first started?

question: What happens immediately after a mature atherosclerotic plaque ruptures inside a coronary artery?

question: What is the best way to give pain medication to a dying patient in constant pain?

question: Which part of the respiratory tract filters out large particles before they reach the lungs?

question: What is a standard chest X-ray most commonly used to check for in the ward?

question: What is the main job of the endocrine system in our body?

question: How do intravenous (IV) fluids like normal saline help a patient with severe fluid loss?

question: What does milking a drainage tube involve?

options.B: Positive Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs
options.C: Profound hyperpigmentation of the skin
options.D: Exophthalmos and a fine hand tremor

explanation: Calcium keeps our nerves and muscles calm. When calcium drops too low, nerves become super jumpy, causing muscles to twitch or spasm during Trousseau's and Chvostek's tests.

question: Why can early diagnosis of genitourinary cancers sometimes be delayed?

options.A: Blood tests usually show completely normal results for years
options.B: Patients refuse to provide urine samples during routine visits
options.C: Tumors in these organs never cause any noticeable signs
options.D: Their early symptoms often mimic common urinary tract infections

explanation: Symptoms like burning when you pee or seeing a little blood can easily be mistaken for a simple UTI, which is why sometimes treatment gets delayed while trying antibiotics first.

question: Why is knowing the location of the dorsal penile nerves important during a circumcision?

options.A: It controls the blood flow to the entire lower abdomen
options.B: It guides where to give a local nerve block for pain relief
options.C: It helps prevent accidental removal of the urethral opening
options.D: It ensures the scrotal skin heals without any scarring

explanation: You've got this! Doctors inject local numbing medication near these dorsal nerves on top of the penis to block pain signals effectively and keep the baby comfortable.

question: Which of the following is an environmental hazard that increases fall risk in older adults?

options.A: Bright, glare-free overhead lighting
options.B: Loose throw rugs on the floor
options.C: Properly fitted rubber-soled shoes
options.D: Sturdy handrails along the hallway

explanation: Unsecured rugs frequently catch on shoes or mobility devices, causing accidental trips and falls. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T24#GNS222_U1_T24_h5)

question: A nurse is teaching an asthma patient how to use an inhaler. What is the best way to make sure the teaching worked?

options.A: Explaining the complex chemistry of the aerosol drug
options.B: Giving the patient a textbook chapter to read at home
options.C: Telling a family member to always give the medicine for them
options.D: Demonstrating the technique and asking the patient to show it back

explanation: Return demonstration is the gold standard of patient education! It lets you watch the patient do it themselves so you know they truly understand the steps.

question: Why are newborns more at risk of drug toxicity from certain medications?

options.A: Reduced plasma protein binding leaves more free active drug
options.B: They consume a high-fat diet through breast milk
options.C: Their kidneys filter medications out of the blood too quickly
options.D: Their liver enzymes work twice as fast as adult enzymes

explanation: Newborns have fewer proteins in their blood to hold onto drugs safely, meaning more active medicine floats around freely. Makes sense when you picture it!

question: Which maneuver should you use to open the airway of a patient with a suspected neck injury?

options.A: Jaw-thrust maneuver
options.B: Neck-hyperextension method
options.C: Lateral recovery position
options.D: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver

explanation: When a neck injury is suspected, use the jaw-thrust maneuver. It opens the airway gently without bending the vulnerable cervical spine.

question: What cultural belief often causes many communities to tolerate domestic violence?

options.A: Immediate community intervention during family disputes
options.B: Universal access to legal education for all citizens
options.C: Equal economic power sharing between men and women
options.D: Normalization of patriarchal dominance and domestic discipline

explanation: You're doing great! In many places, old-school cultural norms wrongly frame male control and physical correction as normal or acceptable.

question: Why is recording how well the patient tolerated the exercise so important for the care team?

options.A: It serves as a legal punishment if the patient is lazy.
options.B: It determines the exact hospital discharge date immediately.
options.C: It stops nurses from having to write shift reports.
options.D: It helps guide future exercise plans and shows recovery progress.

explanation: Tracking progress helps the whole healthcare team decide whether to keep the routine the same or step it up next time!

question: What should you do with a used needle right after giving an injection?

options.A: Leave it on the medication trolley for later sorting
options.B: Drop it directly into a puncture-resistant safety box
options.C: Recap it carefully using both hands on the tray
options.D: Break the needle off and throw it in the general bin

explanation: Never recap needles! Dropping them straight into the safety box protects you and your colleagues from accidental needle-stick injuries.

question: Which patient has the highest risk of developing cholesterol gallstones?

options.A: An elderly male who exercises daily and eats low-fat meals
options.B: An adolescent male eating a high-protein diet
options.C: A young adult female with a low body mass index
options.D: A middle-aged female who lost weight very rapidly

explanation: Great thinking! Being female, middle-aged, and undergoing rapid weight loss are classic risk factors due to hormonal shifts and bile changes.

question: What key tip should you give a patient about finishing their prescribed antiparasitic pills?

options.A: Share the remaining medication with family members who feel itchy
options.B: Complete the entire course of medication even if symptoms disappear
options.C: Double the next dose if you forget to take one pill on time
options.D: Stop taking the pills as soon as your stomach starts feeling better

explanation: Even if the patient starts feeling 100% better, remind them to finish every single pill. Stopping early means some parasites might still be hiding out ready to cause a comeback!

question: Why do non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like hypertension often go unnoticed for years?

options.A: Symptoms only appear after a person reaches retirement age
options.B: They develop silently in the body without immediate noticeable symptoms
options.C: Standard diagnostic laboratory tests cannot detect chronic illnesses early
options.D: Patients refuse to visit primary health centres for routine check-ups

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like high blood pressure creep up slowly without causing obvious pain or distress. That's why routine checks are so important for your patients.

question: What does a rising serum lactate level usually mean for a sick patient?

options.A: Red blood cells are multiplying too quickly in the bone marrow
options.B: The patient is eating too many carbohydrates in their tube feeding
options.C: The kidneys are filtering waste products much faster than normal
options.D: Tissues are not getting enough oxygen and are using anaerobic metabolism

explanation: When cells are starved of oxygen, they switch to an emergency backup energy system that leaves behind lactic acid as waste. High lactate = cells need oxygen!

question: Which of these is a key feature of institutional (hospital) care?

options.A: Complete client autonomy over daily schedules
options.B: Reliance solely on family members for medical tasks
options.C: A controlled and unfamiliar hospital setting
options.D: Delivery of services exclusively inside private homes

explanation: Correct! Institutional care happens in hospitals where routines and environments are strictly managed by the healthcare team.

question: Which of the following actions represents a breach of nursing ethics in reproductive health?

options.A: Discussing a patient's private HIV test result with coworkers in the cafeteria
options.B: Providing confidential contraceptive counseling to an unmarried adult woman
options.C: Reporting a case of child abuse to the appropriate hospital social worker
options.D: Refusing to perform female genital mutilation because it is harmful

explanation: Sharing private patient information outside the direct care team violates confidentiality and patient rights. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T7#GNS216_U1_T7_h7)

question: Why is early initiation of CPR critical during a cardiac arrest?

options.A: It prevents permanent brain damage by maintaining minimal perfusion
options.B: It eliminates the need for any medications or defibrillation later
options.C: It completely cures the underlying heart disease causing the arrest
options.D: It guarantees the immediate return of spontaneous heartbeat

explanation: Brain cells begin to die within minutes without oxygen, so starting compressions quickly buys vital time. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is building a trusting nurse-patient relationship so important for holistic care?

options.A: It allows the nurse to give orders that the patient must follow without question
options.B: It ensures the patient will never complain about hospital food or bills
options.C: It helps patients feel safe enough to share deep fears and personal concerns
options.D: It replaces the need for doctors to visit the patient on the ward

explanation: You got it! Trust creates a safe space where patients feel comfortable revealing the emotional and social burdens that impact their healing.

question: A patient with dementia starts forgetting close family members and frequently wanders away. Which stage do these signs point to?

options.A: Middle stage
options.B: Late stage
options.C: Mild cognitive impairment
options.D: Early stage

explanation: Spotting familiar faces becomes tough in the middle stage, and wandering is a classic behavior to watch out for as confusion increases.

question: A patient with severe bleeding after childbirth is in shock, but blood isn't ready at the bank yet. What should you do first?

options.A: Mobilize family donors for replacement and start rapid IV crystalloids while waiting
options.B: Wait patiently until the blood bank completes routine screening hours later
options.C: Administer strong vasopressors without starting any fluid replacement
options.D: Discharge the patient home with oral iron supplements

explanation: Great nursing judgment! In real clinical practice, we start IV fluids right away and quickly rally family members to donate blood while we wait.

question: Why must nurses strictly follow the doctor's weight-bearing orders during mobility training?

options.A: To prevent the client from building too much muscle too quickly
options.B: To protect healing bones and surgical repairs from excessive stress
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing mobility equipment
options.D: To ensure the client does not burn an excessive number of calories

explanation: Spot on! Putting too much weight on a healing bone or fresh surgery too soon can mess up the repair and cause setbacks.

question: A family member is sitting quietly at the bedside crying after a loss. What is the most caring nursing action?

options.A: Sit quietly beside the family member and offer a comforting presence
options.B: Leave the room immediately so the family can have complete privacy
options.C: Encourage the person to cheer up by remembering happier times
options.D: Administer a prescribed sedative to help the person calm down

explanation: Well done! Sometimes silence and a warm, supportive presence speak louder than any words can.

question: In the PQRST pain assessment tool, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?

options.A: Quietness
options.B: Quickness
options.C: Quality
options.D: Quantity

explanation: Great job! 'Q' stands for Quality. It means asking the patient to describe what the pain feels like—is it sharp, dull, stabbing, or throbbing?

question: What is the term for that exciting moment when a mother first feels the baby fluttering inside her womb?

options.A: Quickening
options.B: Balottement
options.C: Lightening
options.D: Engagement

explanation: Quickening is the mother feeling the baby move for the first time! It's a classic presumptive sign because only she can feel it.

question: What is the normal pH range for human arterial blood?
explanation: The body loves balance! Normal arterial blood pH is tightly kept between 7.35 and 7.45 so that enzymes and cells can do their jobs properly.

question: How often should you check mum's vital signs and uterus during her very first hour after delivery?

options.A: Only once at the end of the shift
options.B: Every hour
options.C: Every 4 hours
options.D: Every 15 minutes

explanation: That first hour is high-alert time for postpartum hemorrhage. Frequent 15-minute checks let you catch any sneaky bleeding early.

question: Why must clinic nurses report unusual or severe side effects (AEFIs) to health authorities?

options.A: To punish the community health worker who administered the injection
options.B: To stop mothers from bringing their babies for future visits
options.C: To investigate vaccine safety and maintain public trust in the program
options.D: To immediately ban all vaccine manufacturing in the country

explanation: Exactly right! Reporting helps health teams track safety, catch batch issues early, and keep parents confident in immunizations.

question: Why is a psychosocial assessment vital for clients with neurologic conditions?

options.A: Nerve damage and brain injury affect thinking, mood, and daily life.
options.B: It is the only legal way to discharge a patient from the hospital.
options.C: Physical therapy cannot start until mental health is fully cured.
options.D: It replaces the need for a standard physical doctor's examination.

explanation: Brain and nerve disorders directly alter a person's behavior, emotions, and interactions, making psychosocial evaluation just as important as physical care. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why do nurses take a baseline set of vital signs when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: To diagnose chronic illnesses right away
options.B: To establish a starting point for future comparisons
options.C: To replace the need for a physical exam
options.D: To figure out the exact date of discharge

explanation: Spot on! Baseline values give you a clear reference point so you can easily track whether your patient is getting better or worse over time.

question: Why do nurses need to check pads and tissues passed by a patient having a miscarriage?

options.A: To calculate the exact weight of the pregnant woman
options.B: To determine if all products of conception have left the uterus
options.C: To prevent the patient from experiencing abdominal pain
options.D: To prove that an induced abortion was performed legally

explanation: Checking the tissue helps us know if everything came out cleanly or if pieces are still trapped inside needing medical help.

question: Which type of injury happens at the exact moment a physical blow or crash occurs?

options.A: Metabolic injury
options.B: Primary injury
options.C: Tertiary injury
options.D: Secondary injury

explanation: That's correct! The primary injury is the immediate damage that happens right at the time of impact, like torn tissue or bruising.

question: Which client situation is a clear indication for a family planning referral?

options.A: A routine request for a three-month supply of injectable contraceptives
options.B: A first-time visit for condom distribution at a primary clinic
options.C: A simple request for general counseling on reproductive anatomy
options.D: A desire for a permanent surgical method like a vasectomy

explanation: Permanent surgical methods require specialized surgical skills not routinely offered at basic primary care posts. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T029#GNS226_U6_T029_h4)

question: What shape is the anterior fontanelle (the front soft spot)?

options.A: Square-shaped
options.B: Oval-shaped
options.C: Diamond-shaped
options.D: Triangle-shaped

explanation: You nailed it! The front fontanelle is larger and diamond-shaped, which makes it a great landmark to spot during an exam.

question: In a regular 28-day cycle, when do we usually check serum progesterone to see if ovulation happened?

options.A: Mid-luteal phase around day 21
options.B: During active menstrual bleeding
options.C: Immediately at the end of menses
options.D: On the exact day of ovulation

explanation: You got it! Progesterone peaks after ovulation, making day 21 the sweet spot in a standard cycle to check if ovulation took place.

question: What is the main goal of taking a detailed sleep history from a patient?

options.A: To prove that the patient is exaggerating their nighttime symptoms
options.B: To immediately prescribe the correct dosage of sleeping medication
options.C: To determine the specific pattern, duration, and contributing factors of the sleep problem
options.D: To eliminate the need for any physical examination or lab work

explanation: Asking the right questions helps us figure out how long the problem has lasted, whether it's trouble falling or staying asleep, and what lifestyle habits might be causing it.

question: Which IV cannula size is usually best when starting a blood transfusion for an adult?

options.A: 14-gauge or 16-gauge
options.B: 22-gauge or 24-gauge
options.C: 18-gauge or 20-gauge
options.D: 24-gauge or 26-gauge

explanation: Red blood cells are delicate! Using a nice wide-bore needle (like an 18G or 20G) prevents those precious cells from getting squashed or destroyed as they travel through the tubing.

question: Why must a triage nurse keep monitoring patients who are waiting in the emergency queue?

options.A: Doctors refuse to see patients without updated charts
options.B: Waiting patients often complain about the slow service
options.C: A stable patient's condition can suddenly get worse
options.D: Hospital policy requires a vital sign check every five minutes

explanation: Illness can change quickly! Someone who looks stable at first triage can crash suddenly and need immediate help. Keep a close eye on your patients.

question: Why might a patient have high blood urea levels even when their kidneys are completely healthy?

options.A: Excess sodium intake stops the liver from processing urea
options.B: Low physical activity always increases muscle breakdown
options.C: Dehydration or a high protein meal can raise it
options.D: Lack of red blood cells forces the liver to make more urea

explanation: Exactly! Urea is easily influenced by what you eat and how much water you drink. If a patient is dehydrated, urea becomes more concentrated in the blood even without kidney damage.

question: Where do you mostly find muscarinic receptors in the human body?

options.A: On the cell bodies of preganglionic neurons
options.B: On parasympathetic target organs
options.C: At skeletal muscle motor end plates
options.D: Inside central nervous system blood vessels

explanation: Muscarinic receptors hang out on target tissues like your heart, smooth muscles, and glands that receive parasympathetic messages. You're doing brilliantly!

question: What is the biggest benefit of nurses and physical therapists working closely together?

options.A: Reduction in the total number of healthcare staff assigned to the patient
options.B: Consistent enforcement of safety precautions and care goals throughout the day
options.C: Faster hospital discharge regardless of the patient's physical readiness
options.D: Elimination of daily nursing assessments regarding patient mobility

explanation: When we are on the same page, safety rules (like how much weight a patient can bear) get followed all day long, not just during therapy hour.

question: Which physical change points strongly to long-term high cortisol levels in Cushing's syndrome?

options.A: Truncal obesity with thin extremities and a moon face
options.B: Rapid, unexplained weight loss accompanied by low blood pressure
options.C: Permanent darkening of the mucous membranes and gumlines
options.D: Severe generalized muscle wasting and profound skin darkening

explanation: Cortisol loves to move fat around—collecting it on the belly, back of the neck, and round face while making the arms and legs look thinner. You'll spot this look easily in practice!

question: After putting in an endotracheal tube, what is the quickest and most reliable bedside check to confirm it is in the right place?

options.A: Measuring the blood pressure
options.B: Checking chest expansion visually
options.C: End-tidal carbon dioxide detection
options.D: Listening to the stomach sounds

explanation: Carbon dioxide only comes out of the lungs! Finding CO2 right after the tube goes in proves it is sitting safely in the trachea and not accidentally down the esophagus.

question: What baseline assessment is most critical to perform and record before starting a gastric lavage?

options.A: Abdominal skin turgor and color tone
options.B: Recent dietary history for the past week
options.C: Vital signs and neurological status
options.D: Detailed psychological background history

explanation: Recording baseline vitals and mental status allows the nurse to monitor for rapid changes caused by toxin absorption or procedural complications like vagal stimulation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why should a nurse gently rotate a PEG tube during routine stoma care?

options.A: To make sure the formula flows faster during meal times
options.B: To allow air to enter the stomach and reduce bloating
options.C: To prevent the internal bumper from sticking to the stomach wall
options.D: To help the external skin opening stretch wider for easier cleaning

explanation: Routine rotation stops tissue from growing over the internal retention bolster, preventing a serious complication called buried bumper syndrome. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient has tiny, pinpoint red spots on their skin called petechiae. What is the nurse most likely to suspect?

options.A: Too much stored iron
options.B: High red blood cell volume
options.C: High white blood cell count
options.D: Platelet problems

explanation: Petechiae are tiny spots of bleeding under the skin that happen when platelets are low or not working right to keep blood vessels sealed.

question: Why do nurses do an evaluation at the end of a care plan?

options.A: To determine if the patient met their health goals
options.B: To calculate the total cost of hospital supplies used
options.C: To assign blame if a complication occurs during recovery
options.D: To write a formal discharge report for insurance companies

explanation: Evaluation simply checks whether your nursing actions actually helped the patient reach their health targets. You're tracking success!

question: Why do nurses give medications through an IV line instead of having the patient swallow a pill?

options.A: It lasts much longer in the bloodstream than oral pills.
options.B: It prevents all known systemic side effects from occurring.
options.C: It is completely painless for every patient receiving treatment.
options.D: It provides a much faster onset of drug action in the body.

explanation: Spot on! Because IV fluids go straight into the bloodstream, the body skips the digestive tract entirely and goes to work right away. You've got this!

question: Which of the following is a core component checked during a psychosocial evaluation?

options.A: Current blood cholesterol and lipid levels
options.B: Bone density and risk for sudden fractures
options.C: Exact surgical history from ten years ago
options.D: Coping mechanisms and stress response habits

explanation: Understanding how a client handles stress and copes with illness is a primary goal of psychosocial evaluations. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h2)

question: What local complication can happen if topical corticosteroids are used in thick layers for too long?

options.A: Complete numbness of the area
options.B: Skin thinning and atrophy
options.C: Excessive permanent tanning
options.D: Rapid growth of thick hair

explanation: Prolonged and improper application of potent topical steroids breaks down collagen in the skin, resulting in thinning, fragility, and striae. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h3)

question: Why must you record it carefully when a client decides to switch their contraceptive method?

options.A: To prove that the previous contraceptive method caused a severe illness
options.B: To calculate the exact daily financial income generated by the clinic
options.C: To prevent inaccurate tallying and avoid double-counting service statistics
options.D: To satisfy legal requirements for changing a patient's legal surname

explanation: You got it! Tracking method switches properly keeps our numbers honest and stops us from accidentally counting the same person twice.

question: A nurse has three different crushed pill medications to give a patient through a PEG tube. What is the correct way to administer them?

options.A: Mix all three crushed pills together in one large syringe of water
options.B: Give each medication separately with a water flush between them
options.C: Crush them together and push them down the dry tube all at once
options.D: Dissolve the pills directly into the hanging bag of liquid formula

explanation: Medications must never be mixed together in a single syringe to avoid drug interactions and severe tube blockage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is a major safety worry for a patient who has lost feeling (protective sensation) in their arms or legs?

options.A: Rapid muscle hypertrophy
options.B: Excessive verbal outbursts
options.C: Sudden loss of hearing
options.D: Burns and pressure injuries

explanation: When patients can't feel hot, cold, or pressure, they won't pull away from a hot stove or shift their weight, leaving their skin wide open to quiet injuries and sores.

question: Why do many cases of breast ironing go officially unrecorded in healthcare facilities?

options.A: Fear of cultural backlash and strict secrecy within communities
options.B: Patients naturally healing within a few days without scars
options.C: Direct government orders prohibiting doctors from asking about it
options.D: A complete absence of physical symptoms requiring medical care

explanation: Because family members enforce strict silence, victims rarely speak out due to intimidation and cultural norms. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T17#GNS312_U1_T17_h2)

question: Which hormones drive early heart and blood vessel changes in pregnancy?

options.A: Antidiuretic hormone
options.B: Estrogen and progesterone
options.C: Insulin and glucagon
options.D: Thyroid stimulating hormone

explanation: You've got this! High levels of estrogen and progesterone relax smooth muscles and help blood vessels grow to support the pregnancy.

question: Why are both FSH and testosterone needed for normal sperm production in males?

options.A: Because both hormones are actually identical chemical substances made by the liver
options.B: Because FSH supports the supporting cells while testosterone drives the overall development
options.C: Because testosterone fights off infections while FSH controls body temperature
options.D: Because FSH stops the growth of body hair while testosterone makes bones brittle

explanation: Exactly right! FSH supports the helper cells (Sertoli cells), while testosterone provides the fuel needed for sperm cells to fully mature.

question: What makes record keeping an essential responsibility for a midwife working in the community?

options.A: It helps track birth rates, complications, and immunization coverage over time.
options.B: It replaces the need to talk directly with mothers during visits.
options.C: It is only required to satisfy strict hospital billing departments.
options.D: It prevents mothers from visiting traditional healers in the village.

explanation: Accurate community records allow midwives to monitor public health trends, catch missed vaccinations, and plan local health interventions effectively. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T14#GNS225_U3_T14_h2)

question: Why is an intestinal infection with Taenia solium often more worrying than Taenia saginata?

options.A: It can cause dangerous tissue cysts if eggs are accidentally swallowed.
options.B: It spreads directly from person to person through casual touch.
options.C: It completely resists standard anti-parasitic medications.
options.D: It produces much larger adult worms in the bowel.

explanation: You got it! T. solium eggs can hatch and form cysts in body tissues like the brain (cysticercosis), which makes them particularly tricky and dangerous.

question: A patient comes in complaining of severe tiredness, unexpected weight gain, and feeling cold all the time. Which hormone issue is likely going on?

options.A: Cushing's syndrome
options.B: Hypothyroidism
options.C: Diabetes mellitus
options.D: Hyperthyroidism

explanation: When the thyroid is underactive (hypothyroidism), the whole body's engine slows down, leading to fatigue, sluggishness, and cold intolerance. Great clinical spot!

question: Your patient is medically ready to leave the clinic, but is terrified to go back to an unsafe home. What should you do?

options.A: Advise the patient to ignore the fear and return home immediately
options.B: Connect the patient with safe shelter and social welfare referral services
options.C: Contact law enforcement to arrest the patient for missing work
options.D: Discharge the patient without discussing housing or safety plans

explanation: Never send a vulnerable patient back into danger. Connecting them with safe housing and social workers is a lifesaver.

question: What does the brain's central chemoreceptor primarily monitor to control breathing?

options.A: Total volume of blood pumped per minute by the left ventricle
options.B: Concentration of glucose dissolved in blood plasma
options.C: Direct measurements of iron levels in circulating red blood cells
options.D: Changes in pH and carbon dioxide levels in cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: Central chemoreceptors act like chemical sensors, checking the fluid around the brain for pH and carbon dioxide to decide how fast you need to breathe.

question: When assessing a patient's chest pain, what should the nurse evaluate first?

options.A: The patient's current employment status and stress level
options.B: The cost of the prescribed medications at the pharmacy
options.C: The exact characteristics, timing, and triggers of the pain
options.D: The patient's family medical history from childhood

explanation: Evaluating the nature, onset, and triggers of chest discomfort helps determine if the heart muscle is experiencing acute ischemia. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T4#GNS213_U1_T4_h8)

question: Why is it better to offer simple, closed choices rather than open-ended questions when talking to a dementia patient?

options.A: It reduces the mental effort required to process and answer the question
options.B: It ensures the patient always drinks water instead of sugary beverages
options.C: It allows the nurse to maintain strict control over the daily routine
options.D: It prevents the patient from changing their mind later in the day

explanation: Think of it like saving phone battery! Open questions can overwhelm a tired or confused brain, whereas 'Would you like tea or water?' is much easier to answer.

question: A patient with a recent stroke begins leaking stool unconsciously. What is the most likely underlying cause?

options.A: Primary infection of the internal anal lining
options.B: Neurological damage disrupting normal bowel signaling
options.C: Complete loss of rectal tissue elasticity
options.D: Severe physical injury to the external sphincter muscle

explanation: Strokes affect the central nervous system pathways that control voluntary bowel function, leading to reflex emptying without conscious control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the main chemical trigger in your blood that tells your brain it is time to breathe?

options.A: Nitrogen gas dissolved in plasma
options.B: High levels of blood glucose
options.C: Carbon dioxide levels in the blood
options.D: Oxygen levels in the arterial blood

explanation: You got it! A buildup of carbon dioxide is the strongest alarm bell your body uses to say 'time to take a breath.'

question: Why is getting an accurate patient weight so important in clinical practice?

options.A: It measures total blood volume
options.B: It is used to calculate safe drug dosages
options.C: It determines the hospital billing category
options.D: It replaces the need for blood pressure checks

explanation: Exactly! Many powerful drugs—especially in children and critical care—are dosed strictly by weight in kilograms to keep the patient safe.

question: Why do vitamin and mineral shortages happen so easily in people living with HIV?

options.A: Due to poor intake, malabsorption, and inflammation
options.B: Because the virus uses up all carbohydrates
options.C: Because antiretroviral drugs destroy vitamins instantly
options.D: Because they drink too much clean water

explanation: Spot on! Gut inflammation and eating less food mean the body struggles to absorb the vital nutrients it needs.

question: What do we call the tight, stiff, and involuntary muscle tone that often happens after a brain injury?

options.A: Contracture
options.B: Spasticity
options.C: Flaccidity
options.D: Atrophy

explanation: Spasticity is when muscles stay constantly contracted and stiff, making it tricky for the client to move or relax their limbs smoothly.

question: Why is unconjugated bilirubin dangerous to a newborn's brain?

options.A: It triggers an immediate allergic reaction inside brain cells
options.B: It dissolves easily in body fats and can cross the blood-brain barrier
options.C: It blocks blood vessels supplying the brainstem directly
options.D: It binds permanently to red blood cells and deprives the brain of oxygen

explanation: Because unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble, it can easily slip across the immature blood-brain barrier in a newborn. Understanding this helps you see why keeping track of bilirubin levels is so vital!

question: How many hours should a patient normally fast before doing a barium meal test?

options.A: Exactly 30 minutes
options.B: 6 to 8 hours
options.C: 24 to 36 hours
options.D: 1 to 2 hours

explanation: You're doing great! An empty stomach for 6 to 8 hours ensures leftover food won't hide tiny ulcers or tumors on the X-ray. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h4)

question: What liquid solution is standard for preserving a skin biopsy sample on its way to the lab?

options.A: 10% neutral buffered formalin
options.B: Normal sterile saline solution
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide antiseptic
options.D: Isopropyl alcohol 70 percent

explanation: Neutral buffered formalin is the go-to liquid fixative. It stops the tissue from breaking down so the pathologist can examine the cells clearly.

question: Why do heavy blocks of text usually fail in community health education programs?

options.A: People prefer listening to long audio recordings instead.
options.B: Ink tends to smudge when paragraphs are printed too close together.
options.C: Medical authorities forbid the use of written sentences on posters.
options.D: Low literacy rates in the target population make reading difficult.

explanation: Many community members have limited reading skills. If your poster is packed with heavy text, the main health message gets lost.

question: Why is it important to let the chest completely recoil (rise back up) between compressions?

options.A: It allows the heart chambers to refill with blood
options.B: It keeps the patient's airway open naturally
options.C: It gives the rescuer time to rest their arms
options.D: It prevents the ribs from fracturing

explanation: Full recoil lets the heart expand like a sponge so fresh blood can flow back in, ready for your next push.

question: Why must you always lower a hospital bed to its lowest position after finishing a bed change?

options.A: To comply with fire safety codes for emergency exits
options.B: To reduce the risk of injury if the patient tries to get out of bed
options.C: To allow the mechanical bed motor to cool down
options.D: To make it easier for the cleaning crew to mop underneath

explanation: You got it! A low bed minimizes the fall distance if an unassisted patient tries to climb out, protecting them from serious head injuries or broken bones.

question: Which hormone from the pituitary gland triggers ovulation right in the middle of the cycle?

options.A: Luteinizing hormone
options.B: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
options.C: Prolactin
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Think 'LH surge!' A sudden spike in Luteinizing Hormone (LH) is the exact trigger that causes the ovary to release the egg.

question: When is a basket stretcher (Stokes litter) most useful during a rescue?

options.A: For moving stable patients down smooth hospital hallways
options.B: During rough terrain, outdoor rescue operations, or hoisting
options.C: For quick transfers from a bed to a bathroom shower chair
options.D: When a patient requires immediate open-heart surgery in transit

explanation: You got it! The cage-like design protects the patient securely when navigating rough paths, stairs, or rocky areas.

question: Why should you give clear practical guidance about death certificates and next steps right after a loss?

options.A: To help overwhelmed relatives navigate the administrative next steps
options.B: To ensure the hospital bed is cleared within ten minutes
options.C: To prevent the family from experiencing any grief at all
options.D: To prove to the family that the nurse is in charge

explanation: Administrative tasks feel impossible when someone is in shock. Clear, gentle guidance takes a huge weight off their shoulders.

question: A patient asks you why he developed gout, considering he loves rich meals and has high blood pressure. How do you explain it simply?

options.A: He has a severe bacterial joint infection passed down through his family
options.B: His kidneys and diet are allowing uric acid to build up crystals in his joints
options.C: His body is manufacturing too many red blood cells instead of white cells
options.D: His blood pressure medication is creating calcium deposits in his bones

explanation: You nailed it! Risk factors like diet, blood pressure, and kidney function team up to let uric acid levels rise, leading to crystal deposits.

question: A patient with a broken hip is placed in skin traction mainly for which reason?

options.A: Preventing deep vein thrombosis in the affected leg
options.B: Immediate rehabilitation and walking exercise practice
options.C: Permanent alignment so surgical repair is no longer required
options.D: Temporary stabilization and comfort while waiting for surgery

explanation: Think of skin traction here as a helpful temporary pause—it keeps the leg steady and comfortable until the surgical team is ready. You're doing great!

question: What is one of the main ways nurses advocate for reproductive rights in everyday practice?

options.A: Financially sponsoring family planning clinics out of their own salaries
options.B: Providing non-judgmental, confidential care and education to all patients
options.C: Refusing to treat patients who disagree with hospital policies
options.D: Changing national health laws through Supreme Court litigation

explanation: As a bedside nurse, your best advocacy tool is treating every patient with respect, keeping their secrets safe, and educating them without any personal bias.

question: During which phase of the cell cycle does a cell make a copy of its DNA?

options.A: First gap phase
options.B: Mitotic phase
options.C: Resting phase
options.D: Synthesis phase

explanation: You got this! The S phase (synthesis phase) is specifically when the cell replicates its genetic material before dividing. Think 'S' for 'Synthesis' or 'Copying'!

question: What is a major safety risk for patients with Pick's disease due to temporal lobe changes?

options.A: Developing sudden and severe bone fractures from walking
options.B: Inability to feel pain when touching hot stove surfaces
options.C: Sudden loss of hearing making them unable to hear fire alarms
options.D: Attempting to eat non-food objects or dangerous substances

explanation: Because of changes in how they experience things orally, these patients might try to chew or swallow harmful objects. Keeping hazardous items out of reach is a crucial nursing priority!

question: Which group of men can be affected by male sexual dysfunction?

options.A: Only individuals with chronic kidney disease
options.B: Only men over the age of sixty-five
options.C: Exclusively adolescent males
options.D: Men across various age groups

explanation: Great job! Sexual health issues aren't just for older men—younger guys can face them too, often due to stress or other emotional factors.

question: When prioritizing health issues in a community, what does 'magnitude' mean?

options.A: The distance from the village to the nearest hospital
options.B: The number of people affected by the health problem
options.C: The total financial cost of medical treatment
options.D: The physical size of the local health clinic

explanation: Exactly right! Magnitude simply tells you how widespread the issue is—how many community members are actually dealing with it.

question: Why do uterine contractions eventually become weaker during a prolonged, blocked labour?

options.A: The uterine muscle runs out of energy from overworking
options.B: The maternal kidneys start retaining excess fluids
options.C: The placenta stops producing progesterone
options.D: The baby's heartbeat suppresses uterine activity

explanation: Think of the uterus like any other muscle in the body. If it keeps pushing hard against a blockage without a break, it eventually gets exhausted and runs out of energy!

question: When comparing two groups in a study, why can't researchers just look at raw averages and stop there?

options.A: Hospital ethics boards forbid the use of raw data
options.B: Raw averages cannot be added together mathematically
options.C: Calculators are not accurate enough for raw numbers
options.D: Differences might be caused by random chance rather than the intervention

explanation: Sometimes numbers differ purely by luck or coincidence! Statistical tests like the t-test help us see if our nursing intervention actually made the difference.

question: Why do nurses use geometric dilution when mixing creams?

options.A: To ensure an even and thorough blend of the active drug
options.B: To remove all the natural oils from the base vehicle
options.C: To speed up the drying time of the lotion on the skin
options.D: To make the final mixture change color as it mixes

explanation: Mixing equal amounts gradually keeps the active drug from clumping up in one spot. It's a neat little trick of the trade!

question: A hospitalized patient refuses to eat, avoids talking to staff, and expresses hopelessness about recovery. Which nursing conclusion is most accurate?

options.A: The patient is using problem-focused coping to solve their illness
options.B: The patient has fully adapted to the hospital environment
options.C: The patient has successfully achieved the stage of resistance in GAS
options.D: The patient is displaying signs of maladaptation and needs psychological support

explanation: Withdrawal and hopelessness indicate poor adjustment to illness, pointing directly toward maladaptation requiring intervention. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient undergoing fertility treatments cries and says she feels like a failure. What is the best first thing for you as a nurse to do?

options.A: Suggest that she stop all medical treatments to save money
options.B: Reassure her immediately that adoption is a very easy alternative
options.C: Provide a quiet space, listen actively, and validate her emotional pain
options.D: Tell her that most of her friends likely faced the exact same issue

explanation: You're a natural! Sitting with patients, listening, and letting them feel heard is what great nursing is all about. Another stellar round completed!

question: Why do we prefer a 'clean-catch midstream' urine sample when checking for a urinary tract infection?

options.A: It contains a higher concentration of red blood cells
options.B: It requires less total volume than a random urine sample
options.C: It eliminates the need for any patient preparation
options.D: It avoids collecting bacteria from around the urethral opening

explanation: By letting the first bit of urine flush away skin germs, the midstream sample gives a true picture of what is actually inside the urinary tract.

question: What is the most crucial instruction for a patient taking a fast-acting sleeping pill?

options.A: Take the medication only when you are in bed and ready to sleep immediately
options.B: Wash down the pill with a glass of evening wine to enhance relaxation
options.C: Double your dose if you wake up in the middle of the night
options.D: Stop taking the medication abruptly after three days of use

explanation: These drugs work super fast! Patients must already be tucked in bed so they don't stagger around the ward and injure themselves.

question: Why is it so important to interview a patient alone when checking for gender-based violence?

options.A: To comply with laboratory protocols for collecting blood samples
options.B: To prevent the abuser from intimidating the patient or blocking disclosure
options.C: To allow the doctor to perform a physical examination faster
options.D: To speed up the hospital admission and bed allocation process

explanation: Spot on! Abusers often tag along to control the narrative. Speaking alone gives the patient a safe space to talk freely.

question: What is the primary purpose of inflammation in the human body?

options.A: To decrease blood flow to injured areas
options.B: To permanently increase the body temperature
options.C: To speed up the breakdown of red blood cells
options.D: To destroy foreign invaders and repair damaged tissue

explanation: The immune system initiates inflammation specifically to neutralize threats and heal injuries. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h1)

question: A young woman presents to the clinic months after a traditional birth procedure complaining of continuous urine leakage and severe social isolation. What condition should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Stress incontinence
options.B: Urinary tract infection
options.C: Kidney stones
options.D: Vesicovaginal fistula

explanation: Continuous, uncontrollable leaking of urine following traditional vaginal cutting is the classic presentation of a vesicovaginal fistula. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T16#GNS312_U1_T16_h4)

question: A patient is prescribed five different medications for chronic illnesses and begins missing doses due to confusion. What is the most likely clinical consequence?

options.A: Automatic resistance to all known classes of surgical anesthetics
options.B: Permanent physical dependence on the prescribed pharmaceutical drugs
options.C: Treatment failure and worsening of the underlying health conditions
options.D: Immediate development of severe drug allergies and skin rashes

explanation: When patients get overwhelmed by complex regimens and stop taking their drugs, their health conditions typically deteriorate. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h3)

question: Which of these is a healthy, adaptive way for a patient to cope with a chronic illness?

options.A: Isolating oneself completely from friends and family
options.B: Seeking social support and talking about their feelings
options.C: Refusing all prescribed medications out of pure frustration
options.D: Pretending that no physical symptoms exist at all

explanation: Reaching out and talking it out helps patients process stress constructively. We all need a support system!

question: Why does an overstretched, fibrous uterus struggle to stop bleeding after delivery?

options.A: It absorbs oxytocin medication much faster than a normal uterus.
options.B: It prevents the placenta from detaching from the uterine wall.
options.C: It lacks the strong muscle tone needed to squeeze open blood vessels shut.
options.D: It cannot produce enough amniotic fluid for lubrication.

explanation: To stop bleeding naturally, the womb needs to contract into firm muscle clamps (often called living ligatures) that pinch the bleeding blood vessels closed.

question: Which sign tells you there might be nerve compression in a limb with skin traction?

options.A: Rapid healing of the skin surface
options.B: Dark brown discoloration of the nails
options.C: Increased warmth and heavy sweating
options.D: Numbness and tingling in the toes

explanation: Numbness and tingling (paresthesia) are classic warning signs that pressure is building up on the nerves. Always listen when patients report these feelings!

question: A client with severe difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) just finished a meal in bed. What is your most important immediate action?

options.A: Brush the client's teeth while they lie flat on their back
options.B: Lay the client flat immediately to help with digestion
options.C: Keep the head of the bed elevated for at least 30 minutes
options.D: Encourage the client to drink a large glass of thin water quickly

explanation: Keeping the head elevated prevents food or liquid from flowing back up and entering the airway, which lowers the risk of choking or aspiration.

question: How often should a bedridden stroke patient be repositioned to prevent pressure ulcers?

options.A: Once every shift
options.B: Only when the patient complains
options.C: Every two hours
options.D: Every six hours

explanation: Regular turning every two hours relieves pressure on bony prominences and protects fragile skin integrity. [learn more](GNS123_U6_T4#GNS123_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which cells in our bones are responsible for breaking down old bone tissue?

options.A: Osteoids
options.B: Osteocytes
options.C: Osteoblasts
options.D: Osteoclasts

explanation: Think of osteo-clasts as the cleanup crew that breaks down old bone matrix, while osteo-blasts build new bone up! You've got this.

question: How did ancient Greek medicine under Hippocrates differ from earlier mystical approaches?

options.A: It prohibited the use of herbal remedies and plant extracts
options.B: It relied entirely on spiritual sacrifices and ritual prayers
options.C: It viewed disease as a natural process rather than divine punishment
options.D: It used modern laboratory testing and surgical antibiotics

explanation: Hippocrates and his followers shifted the focus toward rational observation of symptoms and natural causes of illness. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T2#GNS112_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which factor is most critical for a nurse to verify before initiating provider-assisted partner notification?

options.A: The local government tax clearance certificate of the couple
options.B: Whether the partner owns a smartphone or a television set
options.C: The informed consent and safety status of the index client
options.D: The exact bank balance and employment status of the partner

explanation: Patient safety comes first; partner notification must never endanger the index client or proceed without their explicit agreement. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h6)

question: Which nervous system kicks in when a patient practices slow, deep breathing?

options.A: Central nervous system
options.B: Somatic nervous system
options.C: Parasympathetic nervous system
options.D: Sympathetic nervous system

explanation: Deep breathing signals your vagus nerve to turn on the parasympathetic system—your body's wonderful 'rest-and-digest' mode that cools everything down.

question: How does the team nursing setup benefit junior staff and nursing students on the ward?

options.A: By exempting them from doing any physical patient care
options.B: By allowing them to write hospital policies
options.C: By giving them a supportive environment to learn from senior leaders
options.D: By forcing them to work alone without any supervision

explanation: That's right! Working closely with a registered nurse team leader gives students safe guidance and wonderful practical experience. Every shift is a learning win!

question: Which of these is NOT a challenge that leads to unsafe injection practices in low-resource settings?

options.A: High patient demand for parenteral treatments
options.B: Shortages of single-use sterile injection equipment
options.C: An overabundance of certified auto-disable syringes
options.D: The operation of informal and unregulated drug vendors

explanation: Facilities actually suffer from shortages of safe equipment, not an overabundance! Lack of supplies is a major hurdle.

question: What happens when a baby is born with an imperforate hymen?

options.A: The vaginal canal is divided into two separate channels.
options.B: The vaginal opening is completely blocked by a solid membrane.
options.C: The entire uterus and both ovaries are missing from birth.
options.D: The cervix fails to produce any protective mucus.

explanation: Exactly right! An imperforate hymen means a continuous layer of tissue seals the lower end of the vagina, which prevents menstrual flow from escaping later in life.

question: During a surgical hand scrub, which way should the rinse water flow off your arms?

options.A: From the hands down toward the elbows
options.B: Directly off the side of the wrists
options.C: From the forearms up to the palms
options.D: From the elbows up toward the fingertips

explanation: Always let water flow from clean (hands) to less clean (elbows). This prevents dirty water from running back down onto your freshly washed fingers!

question: Which part of the fallopian tube is the most common site for an ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Ampulla
options.B: Cervix
options.C: Ovary
options.D: Myometrium

explanation: The ampulla is the widest section of the fallopian tube, making it the most frequent place for a fertilized egg to become trapped and implant. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h2)

question: What would an occupational therapist most likely help a recovering stroke patient do?

options.A: Rebuilding leg strength to walk up a flight of stairs
options.B: Practicing how to safely button a shirt and brush teeth
options.C: Navigating financial assistance for home medical equipment
options.D: Adjusting medication dosages for blood pressure control

explanation: You nailed it! Occupational therapists (OTs) focus on everyday tasks like dressing and grooming, while physical therapists focus on big movements like walking.

question: If your rural clinic runs out of official safety boxes, what is a safe, clever backup plan for used needles?

options.A: Using locally available, puncture-resistant rigid containers
options.B: Throwing loose needles directly into the regular dustbin
options.C: Burying uncapped needles in the hospital garden
options.D: Washing and reusing disposable needles for multiple patients

explanation: Improvise safely! Using a sturdy, thick local container keeps everyone safe from needle pricks until official disposal arrives.

question: Which main hormone is dangerously low during an adrenal crisis?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Vasopressin
options.C: Thyroxine
options.D: Cortisol

explanation: Cortisol is our primary stress hormone. When the adrenal glands fail to pump it out, the body struggles to handle even basic stress.

question: Which animal is well-known as the natural reservoir host for transmitting Lassa fever in West Africa?

options.A: Mastomys rat
options.B: Anopheles mosquito
options.C: Domestic livestock
options.D: Migratory birds

explanation: The multimammate rat (Mastomys) carries the Lassa virus and sheds it in homes through its urine and droppings. Good public health detail to keep in mind!

question: Which blood test is the most reliable sign that heart muscle cells have been damaged?

options.A: Troponin
options.B: Complete blood count
options.C: Blood urea nitrogen
options.D: Serum electrolytes

explanation: That's right! Troponin is a special cardiac protein that spills into the bloodstream specifically when heart muscle cells get injured or start dying.

question: Why is it important for a patient to empty her bladder right before an MVA procedure?

options.A: To stop the kidneys from producing urine for the next several hours
options.B: To prevent accidental urine contamination of the surgical field
options.C: To test kidney function before giving any local anesthetic drugs
options.D: To make the pelvic exam and uterine positioning easier and less painful

explanation: A full bladder displaces the uterus, makes bimanual palpation difficult, and increases patient discomfort during speculum and instrument insertion. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T010#GNS226_U5_T010_h4)

question: How does prolonged bed rest and immobility most directly harm the cardiovascular and skin systems?

options.A: It lowers the body temperature to dangerous levels.
options.B: It promotes blood clots in deep veins and breaks down skin integrity.
options.C: It immediately stops the kidneys from producing urine.
options.D: It causes the patient to drink too much water.

explanation: When blood pools from lack of movement, clots form easily, and constant pressure on skin leads to painful, hard-to-heal pressure ulcers. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T4#GNS321_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why is a patient taking long-term steroid medications at a higher risk of getting infections?

options.A: Corticosteroids cause an immediate permanent loss of lymph nodes
options.B: The medication suppresses normal immune and inflammatory responses
options.C: The treatment increases the production of abnormal red blood cells
options.D: The drug directly destroys the protective outer layers of the skin

explanation: Spot on! Corticosteroids calm down inflammation, but in doing so, they also quiet down the immune system, making it harder to fight off everyday germs.

question: Why is gender equity often necessary before gender equality can be truly achieved?

options.A: Equity provides tailored support to overcome existing social disadvantages
options.B: Equality is harmful and should be replaced entirely by equity
options.C: Equity means treating all patients with the exact same standard protocol
options.D: Equity ensures that biological sex differences are completely erased

explanation: Because historical inequalities put certain groups behind, equity steps in with customized help so everyone has a fair chance to reach an equal outcome. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T1#GNS312_U4_T1_h6)

question: Which organ is in the greatest danger during a paracetamol overdose?

options.A: The stomach
options.B: The kidneys
options.C: The liver
options.D: The pancreas

explanation: The liver works hard to break down paracetamol. When too much is taken at once, it gets overwhelmed and can suffer serious damage.

question: Why is continuous electronic fetal monitoring so important during preterm labour?

options.A: Preterm fetuses tolerate the stress of contractions poorly
options.B: It stops the progress of cervical dilation automatically
options.C: It is the only way to calculate the exact due date
options.D: It prevents the mother from experiencing any back pain

explanation: Preterm babies have delicate reserves, so watching the monitor closely helps us catch signs of distress early. You're learning top-tier patient safety!

question: How do infectious bacteria usually travel to cause salpingitis?

options.A: They enter directly through the skin of the lower abdomen
options.B: They spread through the bloodstream from the lungs
options.C: They ascend upward from the lower genital tract
options.D: They travel down from the abdominal cavity through the liver

explanation: Salpingitis is an ascending infection, meaning germs travel up from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and tubes.

question: What is the primary role of the Reticular Activating System (RAS) in the brain stem?

options.A: Processing visual images from the eyes
options.B: Controlling fine motor coordination
options.C: Maintaining wakefulness and alertness
options.D: Regulating resting heart rate

explanation: The RAS is like your brain's alarm clock! It keeps you awake, alert, and responsive to everything happening around you.

question: What is the best reaction when a community nurse discovers a patient is using traditional herbal remedies alongside prescribed drugs?

options.A: Refuse to treat the patient until they sign an apology
options.B: Yell at the patient immediately and throw the herbs away
options.C: Report the patient to local security agencies at once
options.D: Discuss the herbs calmly to check for any dangerous drug interactions

explanation: A non-judgmental approach helps patients feel safe to share their habits, allowing the nurse to protect them from harmful drug-herb interactions. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T10#GNS112_U5_T10_h5)

question: Which of these is a strict 'no-go' (absolute contraindication) for putting in an IUD?

options.A: Mild iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Having had a past cesarean section
options.C: A history of high blood pressure
options.D: Confirmed or suspected pregnancy

explanation: Never place an IUD if a woman is already pregnant! It can cause serious complications, severe infection, or miscarriage.

question: Why are intravenous fluids often ordered for a patient experiencing drug toxicity?

options.A: To instantly neutralize the chemical pH of all oral medications
options.B: To help flush water-soluble drugs out through the kidneys
options.C: To dilute the remaining blood cells in the circulatory system
options.D: To replace liver tissue damaged by the toxic substance

explanation: Hydration supports kidney output, helping the body eliminate circulating toxins faster through urine. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h7)

question: Why should a nurse check a patient's serum albumin lab result before giving a protein-bound drug?

options.A: To measure the exact body fat percentage
options.B: To see how well the kidneys are making urine
options.C: To determine if there is a bacterial infection
options.D: To check if the patient is at risk for drug toxicity

explanation: Low albumin levels change the balance of bound vs. free drug. Checking this lab value helps you keep the patient safe from unexpected high doses of active medicine.

question: What happens inside the body during disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?

options.A: Widespread clotting exhausts platelets and factors, causing severe bleeding.
options.B: The body rapidly produces too many red blood cells.
options.C: Vitamin K is completely destroyed in the stomach.
options.D: Platelets permanently lose their ability to stick together.

explanation: DIC is a wild rollercoaster: the body forms tiny clots everywhere all at once, using up all its platelets and clotting factors. Once they are gone, the patient unfortunately starts bleeding heavily elsewhere.

question: Why is regular skin monitoring necessary while a poultice is in place?

options.A: To catch early signs of thermal burns or irritation
options.B: To measure how much weight the patient gained
options.C: To see if the bandages can be sold again
options.D: To check if the patient is sleeping soundly

explanation: Frequent checks ensure that heat or active ingredients do not damage or blister the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h7)

question: A menopausal patient has vaginal spotting and mild burning. What is the most likely cause of her cervical sensitivity?

options.A: Hyperactive cellular growth in the transformation zone
options.B: Frequent use of harsh chemical douches for hygiene
options.C: Lower estrogen levels causing thinning and drying of mucosal tissue
options.D: Increased production of thick mucus blocking the cervical canal

explanation: Well done! After menopause, lower estrogen makes the tissues thinner, drier, and much easier to irritate.

question: Why is following a strict code of ethics so important for a nurse?

options.A: It ensures the nurse receives the highest possible salary tier
options.B: It eliminates the need for any formal continuing education classes
options.C: It guarantees patient confidentiality, dignity, and fairness in care
options.D: It grants the nurse legal authority to perform major surgeries

explanation: Our ethical code is our compass. It guides us to treat every patient fairly, keep their secrets safe, and always respect their human dignity. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T1#GNS112_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why do patients with heart valve problems often develop a heart murmur?

options.A: The electrical wires in the heart rub against each other.
options.B: Turbulent blood flow occurs as blood moves through narrowed or leaky valves.
options.C: Air gets trapped inside the heart muscle tissue.
options.D: The lungs make whistling sounds during deep breathing.

explanation: Normally, blood flows smoothly and quietly. But when it's forced through a tight or leaky valve, it splashes around and makes a WHOOSH sound—which we call a murmur!

question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency?

options.A: Suppression caused by chemotherapy drugs
options.B: A genetic enzyme defect present since birth
options.C: Immune damage resulting from an HIV infection
options.D: Malnutrition leading to weakened white blood cell function

explanation: A condition present right from birth is a primary (congenital) issue. Conditions like HIV, malnutrition, and chemo damage a previously healthy immune system later in life, making them acquired.

question: What is the main goal of laws and policies guiding waste disposal in healthcare?

options.A: To generate revenue through heavy facility fines
options.B: To make hospital paperwork as complicated as possible
options.C: To restrict the purchase of medical equipment
options.D: To standardize safe practices and protect public safety

explanation: You got it! Laws ensure every clinic and hospital follows clear, uniform rules to keep staff and patients safe.

question: What is the nurse's specific job when handling a surgical consent form?

options.A: Explaining all potential surgical risks and complications in detail to the patient
options.B: Witnessing the patient's signature after confirming they understand the procedure from the surgeon
options.C: Signing the consent form on behalf of an unconscious patient without family
options.D: Deciding whether the patient is mentally fit to undergo general anesthesia

explanation: The doctor explains the surgery, but you act as the trusted witness to make sure the patient understands and is signing willingly. Teamwork!

question: What is the medical term for the excessive thirst that a diabetic patient often feels?

options.A: Polyphagia
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Polydipsia
options.D: Paresthesia

explanation: Polydipsia simply means extreme thirst. It happens because the body is losing a lot of water through frequent urination (polyuria). You are building a solid clinical vocabulary!

question: If you want to share health news quickly in a village, what should you look for first?

options.A: Written laws governing foreign healthcare workers
options.B: Local communication networks and gathering places
options.C: The distance to the nearest major city
options.D: The exact number of brick houses in the area

explanation: Find out where people naturally meet—like markets or community centers—so your health message can travel fast!

question: Which of these is NOT checked during a standard surgical time-out?

options.A: The exact surgical site and body part
options.B: The specific procedure intended to be done
options.C: The patient's preferred religious denomination
options.D: The correct identity of the surgical patient

explanation: While respecting a patient's religion is important for holistic care, it isn't part of the quick safety checklist used to prevent wrong-site or wrong-patient surgery.

question: Which piece of equipment is an absolute must to have right at the bedside after major mouth surgery?

options.A: An interactive electronic speech tablet
options.B: Suction equipment and bag-valve-mask device
options.C: Heavy rubber mouth guards
options.D: Warm saline foot bath basins

explanation: Suction keeps the airway clear of blood and saliva, so emergency tools must always be ready to roll.

question: What is the main cause of an ischemic stroke?

options.A: Sudden systemic drop in normal body temperature
options.B: Uncontrolled electrical discharge across the motor cortex
options.C: Rupture of a weakened blood vessel inside the brain tissue
options.D: Occlusion of a cerebral artery by a thrombus or embolus

explanation: An ischemic stroke happens when a blood clot blocks a brain vessel, cutting off the oxygen and nutrients that part of the brain needs.

question: Which of the following structures is found inside the cranial cavity?

options.A: Lungs
options.B: Spinal cord
options.C: Brain
options.D: Heart

explanation: The cranial cavity is formed by the skull bones and specifically houses the brain. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h2)

question: A woman in labor gets an epidural and suddenly feels dizzy as her blood pressure drops. Why?

options.A: Sympathetic blockade leading to maternal vasodilation
options.B: Direct allergic reaction to the local anesthetic agent
options.C: Premature placental detachment from the uterine wall
options.D: Acute uterine rupture caused by relaxed muscles

explanation: The epidural numbs the nerves that keep blood vessels tight. When those vessels relax and widen (vasodilation), blood pressure takes a quick dip.

question: How do blood vessel (vascular) diseases lead to erectile dysfunction?

options.A: By causing excessive testosterone production in the testes
options.B: By blocking the normal production of seminal fluid
options.C: By destroying the nerves of the cremasteric muscle
options.D: By impairing adequate blood flow into the cavernous tissues

explanation: You got it! An erection needs good, healthy blood flow to fill the tissues. If vascular disease gets in the way, that flow is restricted.

question: Why is good communication so important when an older patient moves from the rehab center back home?

options.A: It prevents confusion and ensures therapy strategies are continued safely
options.B: It is only done to satisfy mandatory government billing forms
options.C: It guarantees the patient will never need medical care again
options.D: It allows the physical therapist to move into the patient's house

explanation: You nailed it! Smooth handover notes and clear instructions ensure family members know how to keep caring for the patient safely at home.

question: What was the main source of medicines used by ancient civilizations?

options.A: Genetically modified crops
options.B: Synthesized laboratory chemicals
options.C: Purified animal hormones
options.D: Plants and minerals found in nature

explanation: Before modern laboratories, early healers relied entirely on natural sources like roots, barks, leaves, and minerals to treat illnesses. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T1#GNS125_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which symptom strongly tells a nurse to check the throat and voice box (larynx)?

options.A: Persistent hoarseness
options.B: Ringing in the ears
options.C: Stuffiness in the nose
options.D: Blurry vision

explanation: Voice changes that stick around for weeks can point to vocal cord bumps, swelling, or growths, meaning it's time for a closer look.

question: A patient develops cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease. What sign might you spot as a nurse?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood glucose levels
options.B: Sudden sharp chest pain and absent breath sounds
options.C: Bright red blood coming up when coughing
options.D: Swollen lower legs and distended neck veins

explanation: Spot on! Since the right side of the heart is struggling to pump forward, fluid backs up into the body, causing swollen legs and puffy neck veins.

question: Which group of medications is most commonly used to manage severe pain and breathlessness in palliative care?

options.A: Antihypertensives
options.B: Antibiotics
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Opioids

explanation: You nailed it! Opioids are the gold standard for getting severe pain and tough breathing under control so the patient can finally rest comfortably.

question: A community health nurse wants to help lower the rate of undiagnosed high blood pressure in a low-income neighborhood. Which activity is the best initial approach?

options.A: Mailing complex research journals to every household in the area
options.B: Instructing residents to buy their own digital blood pressure monitors online
options.C: Waiting inside the hospital clinic for patients to schedule appointments
options.D: Setting up a free mobile blood pressure screening booth at a local community center

explanation: Community outreach brings screening services directly to populations with limited healthcare access, enabling early detection of silent conditions. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why doesn't it work to treat only the female patient while completely ignoring her sexual partners?

options.A: It frequently leads to immediate reinfection of the patient
options.B: It stops the patient's immune system from producing antibodies
options.C: It causes the laboratory tests to show false positive results
options.D: It automatically makes the bacteria resistant to all antibiotics

explanation: It's a cycle! If the partner still has the infection, sleeping together again will just pass it right back to her.

question: Which specific weight change should a patient with heart failure report immediately to their healthcare provider?

options.A: Gradually losing one kilogram over a full month
options.B: Staying at the exact same weight for two consecutive weeks
options.C: Gaining more than two kilograms in a couple of days
options.D: Fluctuating by a few grams after eating a large evening meal

explanation: A rapid weight gain over a short period is a reliable sign of fluid retention and worsening heart failure before other symptoms appear. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h5)
